final_answer: ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE OCCURS WHEN MICROORGANISMS DEVELOP THE ABILITY TO SURVIVE EXPOSURE TO ANTIBIOTICS. THE EVOLUTIONARY MECHANISM INVOLVES NATURAL SELECTION. WHEN ANTIBIOTICS ARE USED, THEY KILL SUSCEPTIBLE MICROBES, BUT ANY MICROBES WITH MUTATIONS OR GENETIC VARIATIONS THAT PROVIDE RESISTANCE SURVIVE. THESE SURVIVING MICROBES THEN REPRODUCE, PASSING ON THEIR RESISTANT TRAITS TO THEIR OFFSPRING. OVERPREScription OF ANTIBIOTICS MEANS THEY ARE USED IN SITUATIONS WHERE THEY ARE NOT NECESSARY, SUCH AS FOR VIRAL INFECTIONS. THIS EXPOSURE CREATES SELECTIVE PRESSURE ON MICROBES, ALLOWING RESISTANT STRAINS TO THRIVE. INCORRECT USE, SUCH AS NOT FINISHING THE FULL COURSE OF ANTIBIOTICS, CAN LEAD TO PARTIAL KILLING OF MICROBES, LEAVING RESISTANT ONES TO PREDOMINATE. THE COMBINATION OF THIS SELECTION PRESSURE AND THE PROPAGATION OF RESISTANT GENES THROUGH GENETIC TRANSFER MECHANISMS LEADS TO THE SPEEDY DEVELOPMENT OF ANTIBIOTIC RESISTANCE. IT IS CRITICAL TO USE ANTIBIOTICS PROPERLY AND ONLY WHEN NECESSARY TO MINIMIZE THE DEVELOPMENT OF RESISTANT STRAINS.
